notes:
I've arranged these notes verse by verse, and every point has its source URL. I couldn't search much, so some sources you asked for are missing; the gaps are listed at the end.

---

**v. 1**
- **The elder:** Gill says this is the Apostle John, calling himself "the elder" because of his age and his office. The elder is the writer of the epistle, the Apostle John, who so styles himself on account of his age, and office — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/3-john/1-1.html
- Guzik says Christians have understood from the earliest times that this is the Apostle John. He suggests John may have avoided naming himself because of the threat of persecution. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/
- Utley says "elder" means the same as "pastor" and "bishop." — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- **Gaius:** Guzik says we can't link this Gaius to the other men of that name in the New Testament, because it was a very common name. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/ The Gospel Coalition commentary also thinks he is probably not Paul's Gaius from 1 Corinthians 1:14. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/3-john/ Wesley disagrees: he thinks this was probably the Gaius of Corinth from Romans 16:23. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
- **"in the truth":** Utley notes that "love" and "truth" often appear together in John's letters. He says "truth" can mean the Holy Spirit, Jesus, or the content of the gospel. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- **Catholic view:** the Catholic Encyclopedia says this Gaius seems to have been not an ecclesiastic but a layman of means. — https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/epistles-of-saint-john

**v. 2**
- **Translation:** the Pulpit Commentary prefers "in all respects" over the KJV's "above all things," adding that John would never have said the latter. It says the Greek word for "prosper" means to "have a good career." — https://biblehub.com/3_john/1-2.htm Maclaren agrees that an apostle would hardly pray "above all things" for someone to get on in the world. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/3-john/a-prosperous-soul.cfm
- **A standard letter greeting:** Guzik says both verbs were everyday letter-writing language, so common that Latin writers shortened the greeting to initials. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/ Utley calls it a typical Greco-Roman opening prayer. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- **Body and soul:** Gill describes a healthy soul as one whose sins are forgiven and which grows on the word in faith, hope and love. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-2.html Matthew Henry: grace will improve health, health will employ grace. — same URL
- **Maclaren's challenge:** would you want to do no better in business than you do in religion? He says the worst adversity is outward success that harms the inner life. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/3-john/a-prosperous-soul.cfm
- **Where views differ (prosperity teaching):**
  - Clarke (Methodist) says every Christian may expect these three blessings (health of soul, health of body and success in daily affairs) "in a certain measure," may pray for them, and would have more of them by praying devoutly. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/3-john/1-2.html
  - Guzik (enduringword, from your charismatic list) says some people wrongly read this as a guarantee of constant wealth and perfect health. God may use a lack of these for eternal good. Yet he also says some live in poverty and disease because they don't seek God's best or walk in faith. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/
  - Chuck Smith says that using this verse as God's promise of healing "is really not scriptural"; it is John's wish for Gaius. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-2.html
  - Utley says the verse can't be used as a proof text for the health-and-wealth gospel. He points readers to Gordon Fee, whom he calls a charismatic scholar. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
  - GotQuestions argues that the context rules out a prosperity reading. In v. 4, John's greatest joy is his children walking in the truth, not their health or wealth. — https://www.gotquestions.org/prosper-and-be-in-good-health.html
  - Steven Cole (bible.org) calls prosperity teaching unbiblical and says this is one of its main proof texts. — https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-3-prosperous-soul-3-john-1-15
  - The Light of Israel commentary says some in the Prosperity Movement treat the verse as a sure cure for poverty and ill health, but John is not making promises. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-2.html
- **"Soul":** Utley says this means the whole person, not a separate part of a human being. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john

**v. 3**
- Wesley explains "the truth that is in thee" as true faith and love. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
- Utley notes that "came" and "testified" are present-tense forms in Greek. This suggests church members or missionaries regularly came back to John with news. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- Guzik: other people noticed Gaius's walk, so they could talk about it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/

**v. 4**
- Wesley: But Diotrephes — Perhaps the pastor of it. That note belongs to v. 9. On v. 4 he says this joy is the spirit of every true pastor, and "my children" is the tender language of a father, whoever actually converted them. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: walking in truth includes sound belief but goes far beyond it. Guzik adds that it means living in line with what you believe, honestly and without pretence. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/
- Utley: Christianity is not mainly a creed or an institution but a life to be lived. "My children" shows either John's authority or his affection. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john

**v. 5**
- Wesley explains "faithfully" as "uprightly and sincerely." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
- Utley: what Gaius did is the exact opposite of what Diotrephes did (vv. 9–10). Gaius helped believers he knew nothing about except that they served Christ. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- Guzik: hospitality may seem trivial to us, but it is love in action. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/
- The Biblical Illustrator says Gaius kept welcoming travellers even after Diotrephes forbade it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/3-john-1.html

**v. 6**
- Utley: "you will do well" was a common Greek way of saying "please." "Send them on their way" was a set phrase for equipping and supplying travelling missionaries. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- Wesley: send them on "supplied with what is needful." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
- Ellicott: the Greek is past tense, roughly "when you have sent them on, it will be a good work." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/3-john-1.html
- Guzik: help people "in a manner worthy of God," meaning excellently. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/

**v. 7**
- **"The Name":** Utley says this stands for the person and work of Jesus. He also notes that John uses the same verb, "went out," for false teachers in 1 John 2:19 and 2 John 7. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- **"Gentiles":** The Gospel Coalition commentary says the Greek word (*ethnikos*) carries a stronger sense of unbelievers opposed to the gospel. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/3-john/ Guzik: other religions' preachers took collections from the public, but these Christian missionaries relied on fellow believers. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/

**v. 8**
- Coffman: those who help missionaries become their fellow workers and share in their reward. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-7.html
- Guzik links this to 1 Samuel 30, where those who guarded the supplies shared the spoils, and to Jesus' promise about a cup of cold water. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/
- Wesley: welcome them "with all kindness." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html

**v. 9**
- **What was the earlier letter?**
  - Barnes says it is lost. He rejects the Vulgate's reading "I would have written." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-9.html
  - Ellicott: possibly John's Gospel, 1 John, or a lost note of no special importance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/3-john-1.html
  - Robertson: probably a short letter of commendation, though some identify it with 2 John. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/rwp/3-john-1.html
  - Gill thinks Diotrephes hid the letter from the church. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-9.html
- **Diotrephes's sin:** Guzik says it was pride. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/ Constable notes that John never says Diotrephes taught false doctrine. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-9.html
- Utley explains the compound word as "love" plus "hold first rank." He adds that the name means "nursed of Zeus." — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john
- **Church government (where traditions differ):**
  - Wesley (Methodist) thinks Diotrephes was perhaps the church's pastor. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
  - Matthew Henry (Nonconformist) calls him a church officer or minister. He notes that John does not summon him to an "episcopal court" but plans to deal with it in the church itself. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/3Jo/3Jo_001.cfm
  - The Geneva notes condemn ambition and covetousness, especially in church leaders. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/3_john/1-9.htm
  - William Alexander (Expositor's Bible) thinks Diotrephes was probably a bishop. He calls the Papacy a "permanent Diotrephes." — https://ccel.org/ccel/alexander_w/expositorjohnepistles.vi.ii.html
  - A preceptaustin compilation calls such one-man control "popery." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/3-john-commentary
- **Catholic view:** the Catholic Encyclopedia says Diotrephes "may have been the bishop" of the church. — https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/epistles-of-saint-john

**v. 10**
- Guzik quotes Boice: the Greek word for Diotrephes's talk comes from boiling water throwing up bubbles, meaning empty talk. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/
- Guzik also says John rebuked him by name in line with Romans 16:17, without stepping outside of love. — same URL
- Henry: ambition breeds malice against those who oppose it. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/3Jo/3Jo_001.cfm
- The Gospel Coalition commentary says such behaviour must be rebuked if the church is to move forward. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/3-john/

**v. 11**
- Wesley: the evil to avoid is in Diotrephes and the good to follow is in Demetrius. "Has not seen God" means he is a stranger to God. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
- **Was Diotrephes a believer? Teachers differ:**
  - A preceptaustin compiler says the verse suggests he "is not from God." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/3-john-commentary
  - Cole says we can't tell whether he was a genuine believer. — https://bible.org/series/1?page=1315
  - The Biblical Illustrator does not take the verse to mean Diotrephes was utterly bad. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/3-john-1.html
- The Gospel Coalition commentary: Gaius needed the warning because manipulation like Diotrephes's works so well that it tempts others to copy it. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/3-john/

**v. 12**
- **Who was Demetrius?** Gill suggests he may be the same as Demas, or the man who carried the letter. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-12.html Barclay thinks he probably led the travelling preachers and carried the letter. The "Contending for the Faith" commentary says it is very unlikely he is the Demetrius of Acts 19. — same URL
- **"The truth itself":** Wesley says it means their testimony is the very truth. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html F. B. Hole (quoted at preceptaustin) says the truth tested Demetrius and he passed. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/3-john-commentary
- **Later tradition:** Utley reports that the Apostolic Constitutions list Demetrius as bishop of Philadelphia and Gaius as bishop of Pergamum. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john

**v. 13**
- Ellicott translates it as "There were many things which I wished to write." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/3-john-1.html
- Guzik: we can share John's preference for meeting in person, but we are glad he had to write. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/

**v. 14**
- Wesley: "by name" means as if John had named each one. The word "friend" is rare in the New Testament because "brother" usually replaces it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/3-john-1.html
- Guzik: the letter is full of conflict yet ends with peace. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/3-john-1/
- Barclay believes the elder's "Peace be to you" brought calm to the troubled church. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-9.html
- Note: some translations split this verse and count 15 verses. — https://bible.org/seriespage/iii-john

**Modern scholarship on who wrote it (v. 1)**
- The 1911 Britannica says 2 and 3 John may fairly be credited to "John the presbyter," a different man from the apostle. — https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/bri/t/the-epistles-of-john.html
- Hastings' Dictionary notes that Jerome and Erasmus held that view, but answers that an ordinary presbyter would not call himself *the* elder. — https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/j/john-epistles-of.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia argues that this separate John the Elder "never existed." — https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/epistles-of-saint-john

**Modern scholarship on what was behind the conflict (vv. 9–10)**
- Barclay sees Diotrephes as speaking for a local church set on running its own affairs. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/3-john/1-9.html
- Robertson thinks he sympathised with the Gnostics. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/rwp/3-john-1.html
- McClintock and Strong suggest he held Judaizing views. — https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/j/john-second-and-third-epistles-of.html

**What I couldn't find**
- No pages from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, or the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org).
- No clear Baptist position stated by a Baptist teacher, apart from Spurgeon on v. 4 (quoted by Guzik) and a MacArthur intro sermon on gty.org.
- My fetch of Utley's commentary stopped partway through v. 7, so it doesn't cover vv. 8–14.
